b: Nondisjunction is the failure of homologous chromosomes to separate during meiosis I, or sister chromatids to separate during meiosis II or mitosis. This is a major cause of aneuploidy (abnormal number of chromosomes).

Cri-du-chat syndrome: Caused by a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p deletion). Characterized by a distinctive high-pitched cry resembling a cat's meow, intellectual disability, and microcephaly.

Klinefelter's syndrome: Caused by nondisjunction of sex chromosomes, resulting in a 47,XXY karyotype. Individuals are typically male with tall stature, hypogonadism, infertility, and sometimes learning difficulties.

qs.q: A 24-year-old medical student is reviewing genetic disorder categories before clinical rotations. What proportion of early pregnancy miscarriages demonstrate demonstrable chromosomal abnormalities?
qs.e: Only about 50% of early pregnancy miscarriages show demonstrable chromosomal abnormalities rather than 100%. This distinguishes early loss etiology from a common misconception that all miscarriages are chromosomal.

qs.e: Approximately 50% of first-trimester spontaneous abortions have demonstrable chromosomal abnormalities, highlighting the importance of chromosomal integrity for fetal development.

qs.q: Which statement about chromosomal abnormalities is correct?
o: Loss and gain produce identical effects
Loss of chromosomal material produces more severe defects than gain
Gain of chromosomal material produces more severe defects than loss
Loss of chromosomal material is better tolerated than gain
qs.e: In general, loss of chromosomal material produces more severe defects than does gain of chromosomal material, which is why monosomies are typically more severe than trisomies.

qs.q: Which THREE autosomal trisomies were among the first chromosomal abnormalities identified?
qs.e: Trisomies 21, 18, and 13 were among the first chromosomal abnormalities identified, along with cri du chat syndrome (5p deletion).

qs.q: What is the clinical implication of 50% of early miscarriages having chromosomal abnormalities?

qs.q: A 2 cm incidental coin lesion on chest X-ray in a 50-year-old shows mature cartilage, fat, and fibrous tissue on biopsy. Cytogenetics reveals clonal chromosomal abnormalities. The correct statement is
o: This is a true hamartoma — a benign developmental anomaly of no clinical significance
This is a pulmonary hamartoma — technically a benign neoplasm despite the developmental name
This is a carcinoid tumour requiring bronchoscopic resection and full staging workup
This is atypical adenomatous hyperplasia requiring CT surveillance every 6 months
qs.e: Clonal cytogenetic abnormalities confirm this is a true benign neoplasm. Despite being called a hamartoma, it is not a developmental anomaly — the name is technically a misnomer.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Chromosomal abnormalities are genetic changes that alter chromosome number or structure, causing developmental disorders or miscarriage. Clinicians must integrate clinical clues, family history, and targeted tests to diagnose and manage these conditions.

sections.p: Chromosomal abnormalities are deviations from the normal 46‑chromosome complement, either numerical (trisomy, monosomy) or structural (deletion, duplication, translocation). Diagnosis relies on karyotyping or high‑resolution chromosomal microarray, guided by clinical suspicion.

t.b: Shows chromosome number and structure; abnormal count or morphology indicates a chromosomal disorder.
Detects submicroscopic deletions/duplications; useful when karyotype is normal but clinical features suggest a microdeletion syndrome.
Prenatal sampling to identify fetal chromosomal abnormalities before birth.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the impact on growth, organ systems, and survival. Early pregnancy loss is the most severe outcome, while milder forms may present with isolated learning difficulties or subtle dysmorphisms.

The leading cause is meiotic nondisjunction, often related to advanced maternal age. Other causes include parental balanced translocations, mosaicism, and environmental factors such as teratogenic exposures.
Presentation varies: early miscarriage, growth restriction, dysmorphic features, intellectual disability, or specific syndromic signs like the high‑pitched cry of Cri‑du‑chat.
Investigations are tailored to the clinical scenario. In pregnancy, invasive sampling is used; in children, karyotype or microarray is first line.

t.b: Elevated in open neural tube defects; normal in chromosomal trisomies.
Pyelectasis, nuchal translucency; increase risk of trisomy 21.

sections.p: Red flags include recurrent miscarriage, multiple congenital anomalies, or a family history of chromosomal disorders. Complications can be severe, such as early fetal demise or life‑threatening syndromes.
Management focuses on treating the underlying cause (e.g., assisted reproduction for advanced maternal age) and providing supportive care for affected individuals. Genetic counseling is essential.

t.b: Used in some cases of Down syndrome to reduce neural tube defects; not routinely indicated for chromosomal abnormalities.

sections.p: Follow‑up includes regular developmental screening and monitoring for associated health issues. Prevention strategies involve preconception counseling and, where possible, IVF with preimplantation genetic testing.
b: Screen for associated cardiac or endocrine issues

sections.p: Chromosomal abnormalities can mimic other genetic or metabolic disorders, such as Down syndrome resembling trisomy 18 features or Klinefelter’s mimicking Turner syndrome.
Low‑resolution karyotyping may miss microdeletions; mosaicism can lead to false negatives; NIPT may give false positives in confined placental mosaicism.

faq.a: Yes, if a parent carries a balanced translocation or mosaicism, they can pass an unbalanced chromosome to offspring.

faq.q: Is there a cure for Down syndrome?
faq.a: No cure exists; management focuses on early intervention, monitoring for associated conditions, and supportive care.

faq.q: What is the role of NIPT?
faq.a: NIPT screens for common trisomies non‑invasively; positive results should be confirmed with amniocentesis or CVS.
